body:
You raise fair points.  I just disagree.

Turchie's affidavit would be fair on this narrow point if it said that both
Kaczynski and the Unabomber used the correct and logical version of the phrase.

The sources of Kaczynski's version ranged from classics like "Ulysses" to the
judges in numerous recent opinions.  In formal writing, one would expect the author
to use it as it appears in literature, and not in common speech (otherwise it would
be a cliche that Kaczynski would prudently avoid).

As to what was redacted below, it would have been the author of the
psycholinguistic comparison, rather than the suspect.  In the early spring, we've
seen that there was a short list of 4 or 5 under 24 hour surveillance.  Then when
they got wind of Kaczynski, they promptly dropped everyone else.


___________________


204. Your affiant is aware that other individuals have conducted analyses
of the UNABOM Manuscript [_redaction_] determined that the Manuscript was
written by another individual, not Theodore Kaczynski, who had also been a
suspect in the investigation.

Boy, I'd love to know what was redacted there.  It certainly sounds as if
the FBI had access to stuff written by someone else who was a good
candidate for the writing, but not for the sending.






vineland repatriate wrote:

> On Mon, 31 May 1999 06:56:53 -0400, Ross Getman <rgetman@twcny.rr.com>
> wrote:
>
> >Karl Kluge wrote:
>
> >>The issue is, if you walked up to 1000 people on the
> >> street and asked them to fill in the blanks in the following sentence
> >>
> >>         you can't <blank> your cake and <blank> it too
> >>
> >> what fraction would say "eat" and "have" rather than the other way around.
> >> As you admit, few people would. That means that the odds that TK and the
> >> Unabomer both coincidentally use it that way is small, supporting a search.
>
> >If that's how it was presented, a judge would have disregarded it .
>
> Why?  It's exactly the same logic as in the presentation of the DNA
> evidence.  There's no sequence data in Turchie, only a statement that the
> DNA known to originate with Ted puts him in a group which could have sent
> the FC documents to Tyler - and that group is quite large, 1 to 5 % of the
> total population.
>
> Honestly, if the DNA workup had been admitted on the simpler inclusionary
> logic, but the cake phrase had been obliged by the legal system to be held
> up - at least rhetorically - as a unique and probative usage, I'd be
> worried about how flummoxed anyone in a white coat could make someone
> wearing the more traditional black robe...
>
> > Instead, in both of Douglas' books and the Turchie affidavit, it was
> >represented as a mistake, peculiar -- unique -- to TK and the Unabomber
> >(albeit in a single-sentence paragraph).   (My view, btw, is that there clearly
> >was probable cause in search of the cabin).
>
> I disagree on how Turchie presented it, unless there's a second invocation
> I missed:
>
> 199. In paragraph 185 of the UNABOM Manuscript (Attachment 2), it is stated
> "...well, you can't eat your cake and have it too." In a letter signed by
> Theodore Kaczynski, to his mother Wanda  Kaczynski, date unknown, Theodore
> Kaczynski compares "... the increase in the complexity of our social
> organization that actually make necessary the erosion of privacy and
> freedom. We will be sacrificing some of the materialistic benefits of
> technology, but  there just isn't any other way. We can't eat our cake and
> have it  too."
>
> 200. It is noted by your affiant that the common use English  Language
> phrase is, "You can't have your cake and eat it too!"
>
> This was the only mention I could find of the phrase in Turchie, and in
> context, para 200 is less important than the similarity in the longer
> passage in para 199 with elements of ISAIF's reasoning.
>
> >I mainly mean to criticize Mr. Douglas, as this sort of "profiling"
> >is his field of expertise.  What's the point of such analysis if it's just flat
> >wrong?  More importantly, why is he including it in a second book many months
> >after the point has been widely made, including in a defense brief?
>
> It does remain an uncommon usage.  I haven't read Douglas so I don't know
> what kind of hay he's making with it.
>
> In general, the Turchie presentation of the textual similarities is pretty
> complicated, and a lot of it relies on material that I don't think is back
> in the public domain - letters from Ted to David and Wanda.  So we're left
> focused on material that is public, and the media were frequently
> presenting the simplest possible explanations of what was being done in
> Turchie's presentation.  The "cake" phrase is one that could be seized on
> as it was simple to explain and uncommon.
>
> A nugget I hadn't caught before in the affidavit:
>
> 204. Your affiant is aware that other individuals have conducted analyses
> of the UNABOM Manuscript [_redaction_] determined that the Manuscript was
> written by another individual, not Theodore Kaczynski, who had also been a
> suspect in the investigation.
>
> Boy, I'd love to know what was redacted there.  It certainly sounds as if
> the FBI had access to stuff written by someone else who was a good
> candidate for the writing, but not for the sending.  A lot of Turchie
> devotes itself to establishing that Ted could have mailed or placed the
> devices on the relevant dates - and presumably their "other individual"
> wasn't a viable suspect to them based on their assumptions that
>
> a) FC was in fact just one person, not a member of any group and
>
> b) their "other individual" could not have mailed or placed documents or
> bombs on at least some of the relevant dates.
>
> -Peter
> scrapie@cyberpass.net
